title: Factorials & Ordered Arrangements
coreInsight: When distinct objects fill ordered positions, the number of available choices shrinks one position at a time, creating factorial products.
targetLearnerRealization: Five distinct objects filling five ordered positions create 5 choices, then 4, then 3, then 2, then 1, so the arrangement count is 5!.
learningObjectives: Build an ordered-arrangement count by multiplying the shrinking number of choices for successive positions.
Interpret n! as n × (n−1) × ··· × 2 × 1 and explain 0! through the single empty arrangement.
Decide whether order and object distinctness make a factorial count valid without adjustment.

continuity.openingCallback: Reuse C1's multiplication principle, but update the number of continuations after each distinct person takes a lineup position.
closingSeeds: When order does not change the true outcome, several ordered lineups may describe the same object and must be grouped together.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Factorial applies whenever objects are selected, even if order is irrelevant.
Repeated or identical objects can be treated as fully distinct without consequence.
Two arrangements with different order can represent the same outcome when the problem ignores order.

beats.purpose: Reactivate C1's multiplication principle and let the shrinking continuation counts emerge from one concrete ordered lineup before any factorial vocabulary appears.
beats.expectedRealization: A filled position removes one distinct person from all later choices, so the factors shrink from 5 to 1.
beats.transitionIn: In C1, you multiplied successive choices when every complete outcome followed each stage. Keep that habit—but now every choice removes one option from the stages that follow.
beats.whyNow: A five-person row is small enough to reason through position by position while clearly exposing why the available choices decrease.
beats.entryBridge: Treat a complete left-to-right lineup as one outcome and count the choices for each numbered position.
beats.exitBridge: The five factors are not five unrelated counts; each records how many friends remain when the next spot is filled.
beats.reusedRepresentation: C1's successive-choice branches compressed into five ordered lineup slots.
learnerPrompts: How many choices are available for the first position?
After one friend is placed, how many choices remain for the second position?
What product counts all completed lineups?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Each lineup follows five successive choices whose branch count decreases by one.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Track the positions from left to right and update the number of unplaced friends each time.

visual.ariaLabel: Five ordered lineup positions with five, four, three, two, and one available choices

steps.title: Start a branch
steps.body: Any of the 5 friends can stand first. Once that choice is made, only 4 unplaced friends can stand second.

steps.title: Keep updating
steps.body: The later positions have 3, then 2, then 1 remaining choice. Every finished lineup follows exactly one such branch.

steps.title: Multiply along the branch
steps.body: C1's multiplication principle counts the complete position-by-position outcomes.

resolution.takeaway: Distinct objects in ordered positions create a product whose available-choice count shrinks by one at every step.

beats.purpose: Make the learner explain the decreasing factors rather than merely copy the product.
beats.expectedRealization: The count shrinks because already placed distinct people cannot be reused.
beats.transitionIn: The product is visible. Now account for why its factors cannot stay at five.
beats.prompt: Why does the second lineup position have 4 choices instead of 5?

options.text: One position has already been used.
One distinct person has already been placed and cannot be reused.
Every multiplication problem must decrease its factors.

feedback.position-used: Using a position matters only because a particular friend now occupies it; it is the unavailable person who removes a later choice.
feedback.person-used: Exactly. The pool of unplaced people loses one member after every placement.
feedback.always-shrink: Factors shrink only when earlier choices remove options from later stages.

beats.correctFeedback: Right—the remaining pool, not the number of stages, controls each new factor.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Ask what changed in the set of people who are still available.

steps.body: The positions stay distinct throughout. What changes is the pool: 5 unplaced friends becomes 4, then 3, then 2, then 1.

resolution.takeaway: A shrinking product is justified only when each earlier choice removes an option from later positions.

beats.purpose: Establish that order must change the defined outcome before an arrangement count is valid.
beats.expectedRealization: Swapping two people creates a different numbered lineup, but would not create a different role-free group.
beats.transitionIn: Distinctness explains the shrinking pool. The word ordered explains why all those branches count as different outcomes.
beats.prompt: Ava–Ben–Chen and Ben–Ava–Chen use the same three people. In numbered lineup positions, are they different outcomes?

visual.ariaLabel: Two lineups containing the same people with Ava and Ben in different numbered positions

options.text: Yes, because Ava and Ben occupy different positions.
No, because the same three people appear.

feedback.different: Yes. A numbered lineup records who occupies each position, so the swap changes the outcome.
feedback.same: That would be true for a role-free group, but a lineup records positions as well as membership.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. In a lineup, membership and position both belong to the outcome.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compare who is first and who is second, not only which names appear.

steps.body: The two rows use the same set of names, but first and second are different roles. Swapping Ava and Ben changes both role assignments.

resolution.takeaway: Count different orders separately only when position or sequence is part of the outcome.

beats.purpose: Attach standard notation to the shrinking product the learner has already constructed and explained.
beats.expectedRealization: Factorial is shorthand for the full descending product, not a new counting rule detached from the slots.
beats.transitionIn: You have already built and justified the product. Now give this recurring descending pattern its compact name.
beats.name: Factorial
beats.conciseDefinition: For a positive integer n, n! is the product n × (n−1) × ··· × 2 × 1.
beats.memoryHook: Factorial records the countdown of available choices when n distinct objects fill all n ordered positions.

beats.purpose: Ground 0! in the empty arrangement so the value is meaningful rather than arbitrary.
beats.expectedRealization: There is exactly one way to arrange no objects: leave the lineup empty.
beats.transitionIn: The countdown ends at one. Push the same arrangement question one step farther: what happens when there is nothing to place?
beats.prompt: How many completed arrangements can be made from zero objects?

feedback.zero: There are no nonempty arrangements, but there is one completed way to place every object: place nothing.
feedback.one: Yes. The empty row is one valid completed arrangement.
feedback.undefined: The arrangement interpretation still makes sense: all zero objects have been placed exactly once.

beats.correctFeedback: Right. One empty outcome keeps the arrangement count consistent.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Distinguish 'no objects inside the outcome' from 'no outcome at all.'

visual.ariaLabel: One empty row representing the single arrangement of zero objects

steps.body: The instruction 'place every object' is already complete when there are no objects. The empty row is one outcome, not zero outcomes.
This also preserves the factorial step n! = n×(n−1)! at n=1.

resolution.takeaway: Zero objects have one empty arrangement, so 0! = 1.

beats.purpose: Separate situations counted directly by factorial from selections or repeated-object arrangements that need different reasoning.
beats.expectedRealization: A direct n! count requires n distinct objects filling n ordered positions.
beats.transitionIn: Factorial is powerful because its conditions are precise. Test those conditions before using the shorthand.
beats.prompt: Sort each situation by whether n! directly counts the outcomes.

items.text: Arrange 5 distinct photos across 5 numbered frames.
Record the complete finishing order of 6 distinct runners.
Choose 3 of 5 students for a committee with no roles.
Arrange tiles R, R, and B when the two red tiles look identical.

response.feedback: Check both conditions: are all objects distinct, and does changing their order change the outcome?

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Distinct objects plus ordered positions make the full factorial count direct.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Use the two-part test: distinct objects, and order that matters.

cases.label: Needs another step
items: R, R, B: two objects are identical

visual.ariaLabel: Four situations grouped by whether factorial directly counts their outcomes

steps.body: The photo and race outcomes record a position for every distinct object, so every order is genuinely different.
Reordering a committee does not change its members, and swapping identical red tiles does not change what is visible. A raw factorial repeats outcomes in both situations.

resolution.takeaway: Use n! directly for n distinct objects in n ordered positions; otherwise inspect what the outcome actually remembers.

beats.purpose: Expose how identical objects collapse labeled orders without turning the lesson into the later general overcounting technique.
beats.expectedRealization: Swapping two identical objects creates a second description but not a second visible arrangement.
beats.transitionIn: One failed condition deserves a closer look. Temporarily label identical objects, then erase the labels and watch what merges.
beats.prompt: Tiles R₁, R₂, and B have 3! = 6 labeled orders. If the subscripts are erased so the red tiles look identical, how many visibly different rows remain?

response.feedback: List rows by the position of the blue tile; swapping R₁ and R₂ changes no visible row.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. The blue tile can occupy any of three positions, and the red tiles fill the rest indistinguishably.
beats.incorrectFeedback: After erasing subscripts, compare rows by color rather than by hidden labels.

visual.ariaLabel: Six labeled tile orders grouped into three visible rows after the red labels are erased

steps.title: Count labeled descriptions
steps.body: Treating the two reds as R₁ and R₂ produces six orders.

steps.title: Erase invisible information
steps.body: Within each displayed pair, swapping the red labels leaves the same color row. The six descriptions collapse to three visible outcomes.

resolution.takeaway: Factorial counts labeled orders; identical objects can make several labeled orders describe the same visible arrangement.

beats.purpose: Transfer factorial meaning from arrangements to an algebraic equation while preserving the descending-factor structure instead of evaluating huge products.
beats.expectedRealization: Regrouping 5! as 12×10 lets 10 join 9! to form 10!, so N=10.
beats.transitionIn: You can now read every factorial as a shrinking run of choices and know when that run counts arrangements. An AMC problem uses the same run as an algebraic object.
beats.transitionOut: The useful move was not brute-force evaluation; it was seeing how one factorial grows from the previous one.
beats.whyNow: The notation is meaningful now, so the learner can exploit adjacent factorial structure without confusing the equation for the source of the definition.
beats.entryBridge: Expand only the factors that help match the 12 and build the next rung above 9!.
beats.exitBridge: Return to arrangements with the habit of exposing only the shrinking factors a problem actually needs.
beats.reusedRepresentation: The descending choice counters become factor tiles that can be regrouped and extended by one rung.
learnerPrompts: What descending product does each factorial stand for?
Which factors inside 5! multiply to 12, and what factor remains?
What factorial is created when that remaining factor joins 9!?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Regrouping exposes 10×9! = 10! without evaluating either large factorial.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Look inside 5! for 4×3, then track the factors left over.

steps.title: Open only 5!
steps.body: Inside 5×4×3×2×1, the factors 4 and 3 make the coefficient 12. The remaining factors make 10.

steps.title: Build the next factorial
steps.body: The leftover 10 is exactly the next factor above 9!, so 10×9! is 10!.

steps.title: Match the equation
steps.body: Both sides are 12 times a factorial, so N! = 10! and the positive integer N is 10.

resolution.takeaway: Factorials grow one rung at a time: (n+1)! = (n+1)×n!.

beats.purpose: Shift from guided distinctions to independent outcome-definition and shrinking-product decisions.
beats.expectedRealization: Each problem begins by deciding whether positions, roles, or visible differences make order matter.
beats.transitionIn: The notation is compact, but the reasoning still begins with the outcome. Use that test independently across five variations.
beats.heading: Independent practice
beats.body: For each problem, define one outcome first. Then decide whether to use a full factorial, a partial shrinking product, or a smaller count because some orders are indistinguishable.

beats.purpose: Verify direct use of factorial on a fresh full arrangement of distinct objects.
beats.expectedRealization: Six distinct books filling all six ordered shelf positions produce 6! arrangements.
beats.transitionIn: Begin with the clean factorial case: every object is distinct and every shelf position matters.
beats.whyNow: This near-transfer item checks whether the learner can independently recognize the exact conditions for direct factorial use.
beats.entryBridge: Count the choices for successive shelf positions.
beats.exitBridge: The entire descending run appears because every book is placed.
learnerPrompts: Does changing their left-to-right order change the display?

visual.ariaLabel: Six ordered shelf positions with a descending product equal to 720

steps.body: Each placed book is unavailable later, so the choice counts descend from 6 to 1.

resolution.takeaway: A full arrangement of six distinct books is counted directly by 6!.

beats.purpose: Extend the shrinking-choice idea to fewer ordered roles than available people without forcing full factorial notation.
beats.expectedRealization: Three distinct medal roles filled from five finalists produce 5×4×3 outcomes.
beats.transitionIn: Now stop the shrinking product early because only three of the five finalists receive ordered roles.
beats.whyNow: The near variation checks that factorial meaning is stronger than mechanically writing 5! whenever five people appear.
beats.entryBridge: Gold, silver, and bronze are three different positions, but there are only three placements to make.
beats.exitBridge: The product stops at 3 because the fourth and fifth finalists receive no recorded position.
learnerPrompts: How many choices are there for gold?
After gold and silver are assigned, how many choices remain for bronze?

visual.ariaLabel: Gold, silver, and bronze positions with five, four, and three choices

steps.body: There are 5 gold choices, 4 remaining silver choices, and 3 remaining bronze choices.

resolution.takeaway: Use the shrinking-position product even when it stops before reaching 1.

beats.purpose: Require an independent count of a repeated-object arrangement using visible distinctions rather than a raw factorial.
beats.expectedRealization: Choosing positions for the distinct blue and green flags uniquely determines the two identical red positions.
beats.transitionIn: The next row still has four positions, but not four distinct objects. Count only decisions that change the visible result.
beats.whyNow: This mixed item checks whether the learner repairs the identical-object misconception with a constructive count rather than repeating 4!.
beats.entryBridge: Place the blue flag, then the green flag; the two remaining positions must be red.
beats.exitBridge: No hidden label on a red flag creates an extra visible arrangement.
learnerPrompts: How many visible choices are there for the blue flag's position?
Once blue and green are placed, is there any remaining red decision?

groups.label: Place the distinct colors
groups.pattern: blue position → green position → reds fill the rest

visual.ariaLabel: Four flag positions counted by placing blue, then green, then the two identical red flags

steps.body: Blue has 4 possible positions. Green then has 3. The two leftover positions receive identical red flags in just one visible way.

steps.title: Connection
steps.body: If the red flags were temporarily labeled, 4! would count each visible row twice—once for each hidden red-label order—so 24 ÷ 2 also gives 12.

resolution.takeaway: When objects are identical, count choices that change the visible arrangement; invisible swaps do not create new outcomes.

beats.purpose: Test whether the learner checks order relevance instead of applying factorial to every selection.
beats.expectedRealization: A three-person committee chosen from four is determined by the one person omitted, so there are four outcomes.
beats.transitionIn: This time every person is distinct, but the result records membership and no positions. Decide what an outcome remembers.
beats.whyNow: The role-free committee directly targets the belief that distinct selected people automatically imply a factorial count.
beats.entryBridge: Look for a description that names each committee once without assigning an order.
beats.exitBridge: Choosing who sits out creates four complete, non-overlapping cases.
learnerPrompts: Does listing the same three names in a new order create a new committee?
What single omitted person determines the committee?

visual.ariaLabel: Four three-person committees indexed by the one person who sits out

steps.body: Each committee is determined by exactly one omitted person, and the four sit-out cases cover every committee without overlap.

resolution.takeaway: Distinct people do not guarantee a factorial count; order must also change the outcome.

beats.purpose: Combine a small case choice with a factorial arrangement of the remaining distinct objects.
beats.expectedRealization: The two special artifacts can occupy the ends in two orders, while the other four fill the middle in 4! ways.
beats.transitionIn: Finish by combining C1's stage structure with today's factorial: settle the constrained ends, then arrange the remaining middle.
beats.whyNow: The challenge asks the learner to decompose a constrained arrangement without introducing a new technique beyond multiplication and factorials.
beats.entryBridge: First choose which special artifact goes on the left end; the other is then forced to the right end.
beats.exitBridge: Each of the two end orders supports all 4! middle arrangements.
learnerPrompts: How many orders can the Sun and Moon artifacts take on the two ends?
How many ways can the other four distinct artifacts fill the middle positions?

visual.ariaLabel: Two end-position cases, each with four factorial arrangements of the middle artifacts

steps.title: Arrange the ends
steps.body: Sun and Moon can occupy left-right ends in 2 orders.

steps.title: Arrange the middle
steps.body: For either end order, the other four distinct artifacts fill the four middle spots in 4! ways.

steps.title: Combine the stages
steps.body: Each end order supports every middle arrangement.

resolution.takeaway: Handle a constraint first, then apply factorial only to the distinct objects and ordered positions that remain.

beats.purpose: Consolidate the lesson's decision process and exceptional base case before the forward hook.
beats.expectedRealization: A reliable factorial count follows from a shrinking-choice argument plus checks for order, distinctness, and the empty case.
beats.transitionIn: Collect the checks that made every count trustworthy before asking what happens when order stops mattering.
beats.prompt: Which statements belong in a reliable factorial-arrangement toolkit? Select all four.

options.text: Track how earlier placements reduce later choices.
Check whether changing order changes the outcome.
Check whether all objects being permuted are distinguishable.
Remember that the empty arrangement gives 0! = 1.
Use n! whenever a problem mentions n objects.

response.feedback: The number of mentioned objects alone is not enough; the outcome definition controls the count.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Those four checks connect the notation to the arrangement it counts.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Reject any rule that ignores positions, repeated objects, or the way choices shrink.

visual.ariaLabel: A factorial toolkit showing the shrinking product, order and distinctness checks, and the empty arrangement

resolution.takeaway: Factorial notation compresses a justified shrinking-choice count; it does not replace defining the outcomes.

beats.purpose: Create the unresolved question that leads from ordered arrangements to C6's overcounting and symmetry.
beats.expectedRealization: If several orders represent one true outcome, the factorial count contains structured duplicates that need to be grouped.
beats.transitionIn: Your factorial count is now secure when every order is a different outcome. Let that assumption fail on purpose.
beats.prompt: Six ordered name cards—ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA—are all different lineups. If the task only chooses the role-free group {A, B, C}, how many descriptions belong to that one outcome, and how might we correct a larger ordered count?
beats.takeaway: Next, we will group ordered descriptions that mean the same thing and use their symmetry to repair overcounts.

notes: Draft foundation lesson authored with the repository-local mathinking-lesson Skill and the compact C3 context packet.
The generated five-friend lineup creates discovery because its shrinking choices expose factorial structure before notation is introduced.
The approved AMC 8 2020 Problem 12 is integrated only after factorial meaning and boundaries are established, using its existing controlled regrouping animation.
The repeated-object examples remain concrete and prepare overcounting without replacing C6's later general symmetry argument.
All declarative visuals reuse existing generic primitives; no lesson-specific renderer behavior was added.
